feedback: If the second half is sketched freehand and roughly opposite, return to counting squares: the reflected feature must be the SAME distance out, not approximately mirrored. Then fold to confirm.
If one or two points are a square off, don't reteach reflection — just re-count that point, mark the equal perpendicular squares on both sides, and fold to self-correct.

If the completed half folds onto the original everywhere (allowing for small folding inaccuracies), that is good evidence the figure is symmetric; the equal square-counts on both sides are what justify it.
activities.intendedInsight: Reflection sends each point perpendicular to the mirror line to an equal distance on the far side; building partner-by-partner (counting equal perpendicular distances) and folding to check turns a 'looks about right' sketch into a construction you can justify and check.
learnerActions: Start from half a butterfly drawn on squared paper beside a clearly marked vertical mirror line.
For each key point of the given half (e.g. a wingtip), count the squares perpendicular from the mirror line to that point.
Count the SAME number of squares straight out on the far side, perpendicular to the mirror, and mark the partner point.
Repeat for every corner/key point, then join the partners in the SAME order as the original half.

Fold the paper along the mirror line (holding it up to the light if needed), or stand a mirror/Mira on the line and compare the reflection of the given half with your drawn half. Check that the two halves line up, allowing for small inaccuracies in drawing and folding.
If the fold misses anywhere, find the slipped point, re-count its squares on both sides, and correct it.
activities.title: Build the butterfly's missing wing, point by point

feedback: If a learner duplicates or shifts an on-the-line point, note its distance from the line is zero, so its partner is itself.
If horizontal or sloping mirrors cause trouble, re-state the rule as 'perpendicular to the mirror, equal distance' rather than 'straight across', so it transfers to any direction.
A fold that fails for a sloping mirror helps show where a partner point was misplaced, so you can re-count that point's perpendicular distance.
activities.intendedInsight: The 'perpendicular and equidistant' rule is constant whatever the mirror's orientation; points on the line are fixed, and the method generalises from vertical to horizontal and sloping lines.
learnerActions: Work a figure that has a key point sitting right ON the mirror line; decide where its partner goes (it stays put — distance zero, not duplicated or shifted).
Complete a figure whose mirror line is HORIZONTAL, counting squares perpendicular to that line (now up/down).

Later, try a figure with a SLOPING mirror line (on squared paper, a diagonal line at 45°), keeping the same rule: each partner the same perpendicular distance from the line, counted in corner-to-corner diagonal steps across the squares.
Fold (or imagine the fold) along each mirror line to check the halves coincide.
activities.title: Points on the line, and new mirror directions

feedback: If you choose the slid (same-orientation) copy, notice both halves face the SAME way, so it cannot be a reflection; fold it and the wingtips miss.
If you choose the version with a point one square off, re-count that point's perpendicular distance from the mirror on both sides; a fold would fail just at that point.

Recognising correct completions and predicting whether a fold would match confirm your understanding, but they do not by themselves make you build and fold your own figure, so pair them with at least one hands-on completion.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to recognise correct reflections — and name exactly why the slid-copy and one-square-off versions are wrong — consolidates the perpendicular-equidistant and sense-reversal rules.
learnerActions: On a grid, complete a given half by marking the partner points and joining them.
From several completed figures, pick the correctly reflected one, rejecting a wrong version that is the half slid across (same orientation) and another where a point is one square off.
Decide whether folding a figure along the mirror line would make the halves match, and say yes or no.
Justify each choice by counting squares or by predicting the fold.
activities.title: Check and choose: deciding if a completion is correct
